eventCatalog.name: Snow: the clock starts
eventCatalog.text: Snow stopped falling. The law gives you 4 hours in the daytime, or until 11 AM after an overnight fall, to open a 4-foot path along your whole frontage. Sanitation agents are out writing tickets.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NOAA daily snowfall at Central Park (GHCN-Daily station USW00094728, element SNOW >= 0.1 in) and the hour the snow ended; DSNY Snow Alert notices
eventCatalog.realFrequency: About 11 days a season with measurable snow at Central Park, 1991-2020 normals (Dec 2.1, Jan 3.7, Feb 3.2, Mar 2.0). The 2025-26 winter brought 43.4 inches, the most in 11 years (CBS New York).
eventCatalog.note: The deadlines are DSNY's. The $30 is one snowfall of the staff option: 1.5 hours at $17.00 plus ice melt. The 0.85 day multiplier is the snow value already in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json; this event adds the duty and the ticket, not a second drop.

eventCatalog.name: Black ice at the door
eventCatalog.text: Yesterday's slush froze overnight. If your stretch of sidewalk is the icy one, people cross the street instead of walking past your window, and the first fall is yours to answer for.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Central Park snow depth above zero (GHCN SNWD) with a daily low at or below 32°F on the days after a snowfall; NWS Special Weather Statement for black ice
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows most snowfalls: January's normal low at Central Park is 27.8°F and February's 29.6°F, so slush refreezes overnight for one to three nights. In January-February 2026 the cold after the January 25 storm kept ice on sidewalks for more than a week.
eventCatalog.note: The user's own example. No study measures how many passers-by avoid an icy storefront; 0.85 on icy days for a shop that did not clear is my estimate, set equal to the snow-day drop. Month value: 3 icy days x 15% / 30 = 1.5%, rounded to 0.98. A shop that cleared its walk gets no penalty.

eventCatalog.name: Letter from a lawyer: someone fell on your ice
eventCatalog.text: A pedestrian slipped in front of your shop on a day you did not clear the snow. Their lawyer has written to the building owner, and your lease says you pay the owner back.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Not a public signal: the claim follows from the player's own record. It is created when a snowfall deadline passed with snow_ice_plan = none (or the shortcut on) and arrives two to four months later
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The Hartford, 2025: slips, falls and customer injuries are 20% of small-business liability claims, twice the 2015 share; the average claim is $45,000 and the average liability claim $97,200.
eventCatalog.note: Deterministic by rule 4: the claim exists only if the walk was left uncleared, and only once per winter. $2,500 = deductible and legal time (planning value); the 25% premium increase for a year after a paid claim is my estimate, no public rate table was found. A court can only hold the tenant itself liable if the lease or its own shoveling made things worse (Cruz v Heights Broadway, First Department 2023); the usual route is the lease's indemnity clause.

eventCatalog.name: Slush on the floor
eventCatalog.text: Every customer walks in with snow on their boots. By ten o'clock the tile by the door is a skating rink, and the line stands right on it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Any day with rain or snow in the forecast (NWS point forecast for New York, NY); days with precipitation of 0.01 in or more at Central Park
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Central Park has about 10 to 11 days with precipitation in every month of the year (1991-2020 normals).
eventCatalog.note: The quality effect is a design value. The money risk sits in the wet_floor_fall_claim record: with 'nothing' chosen through a whole winter the engine raises one claim, as with the sidewalk.

eventCatalog.name: Blizzard warning: the city tells people to stay home
eventCatalog.text: A foot or more of snow is forecast. Schools go remote, above-ground trains may stop, and the mayor asks everyone to stay off the roads. Half your staff cannot get in and the street is empty.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NWS New York (OKX) Winter Storm Warning or Blizzard Warning for New York (Manhattan) County; NYC Emergency Management travel advisory; MTA service alerts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Two in the 2025-26 winter: January 25, 2026 (11.4 inches in Central Park, a record for the date) and a February 2026 blizzard (19.7 inches, ninth largest on record). Many winters have none: the 2022-23 season had 2.3 inches in total.
eventCatalog.note: The deck's 'storm' day is 0.7; a warned blizzard is worse. 0.4 on the storm day and the day after is my estimate from Foursquare's 'up to 40% drop in major weather events' (already cited in nyc-climate.json) and Placer.ai's 20-30% storm-week losses in the hardest-hit states. Month value: 2 days x 60% / 30 = 4%. Delivery falls too: the city has suspended e-bike delivery during the worst hours of past storms. The 2022-23 total is from memory and needs a check.

eventCatalog.name: Ice melt sold out
eventCatalog.text: A storm is two days away and every hardware store within a mile is out of rock salt. Shops that bought their bags in November are fine. The rest are shoveling twice and hoping.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Local hardware store and distributor stock reports before a forecast storm; New York State road-salt contract prices (OGS award: $52.87-$99.90 a ton for 2025-26, average $72.32)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: January and February 2026: stores in the Hudson Valley and Yonkers sold out before the storms and blamed their distributors (News 12); shortages were reported across the Northeast and Midwest.
eventCatalog.note: The contractor option of snow_ice_plan is immune (the crew brings its own salt). For the staff option the engine adds a second shoveling pass and a marked-up bag: $60 is a planning value. No retail price per 50 lb bag in New York in 2026 was found.

mechanics.title: The sidewalk is yours: a legal clock after every snowfall
mechanics.playerDecision: A standing order for December-March (lever snow_ice_plan): staff shovel on the clock, a seasonal contractor, or nothing. On a blizzard day a second order (storm_day_policy): open with a skeleton crew or close.
mechanics.engineMath: The weather series already marks snow days. For each snow day d the engine sets a deadline from the hour the snow stopped (weather seed gives the hour; daytime 7:00-16:59 -> d + 4 h; 17:00-20:59 -> + 14 h; overnight -> 11:00 next morning). staff_shovel: cost = 1.5 h x wage + $5 ice melt per snow day, and one worker is off the bar for that time (capacity that hour -1). contractor: flat monthly fee, no capacity loss. none: (1) violation snow_ice_not_cleared is open from the deadline until the ice is gone (snow depth 0 or three days above freezing): any sanitation inspection or 311 complaint in that window finds it; second and third tickets in one winter use the higher steps $150 and $250-$350; (2) footTraffic at this door x 0.85 on those days; (3) the first such window of the winter creates one sidewalk_fall_claim that lands 60-120 days later. No dice: every branch follows from the weather series and the order.
fieldsNeeded: weather day: hour the precipitation ended
weather day: snowDepth and refreeze flag

numbers.what: Hours to clear when snow stops 7:00 AM-4:59 PM
Hours to clear when snow stops 5:00 PM-8:59 PM
Deadline hour when snow stops 9:00 PM-6:59 AM
Minimum width of the cleared path, feet
Fine steps, USD: first, second, third offense (DSNY page; flyer gives up to 150 / 350 / 350)
Summonses for uncleared sidewalks after the January 25, 2026 storm
Average slip, fall or customer injury claim, small business, USD, 2025
Days a season with measurable snow, Central Park, 1991-2020

extra.howNumbersWereChecked: This session could run web searches but could not open pages: the cloud environment's network policy refused www.nyc.gov, codelibrary.amlegal.com and every other outside host. So no number here is 'verified' in the strict sense of PACK.md (opened the primary source myself). Every record is 'estimate' and carries an 'evidence' field: 'official_excerpt' = the search tool quoted the number from the official page named in 'source' (agency page, law text, court decision); 'secondary' = news, trade press, insurer or vendor report; 'calc' = my arithmetic or a game-design value, with the calculation in 'note'. A person or an agent with open network access can turn every 'official_excerpt' into 'verified' by opening the link.

claims.name: Pedestrian falls on your uncleared sidewalk
claims.law: NYC Administrative Code §7-210 (owner liable); the lease passes the cost to the tenant; CPLR §214 (three years to sue)
claims.trigger: A snowfall deadline passed with snow_ice_plan = none or the shortcut skip_snow_clearing on; at most one claim per winter
claims.note: Average claim $45,000: The Hartford 2025 review of small-business claims (slip, fall or customer injury; $20,000 in 2015). $2,500 (deductible and legal time) and the 25% premium increase are planning values: no public rate table was found. Under Cruz v Heights Broadway (First Department, 2023) the Administrative Code makes a tenant clear snow but does not make it liable in tort; the tenant pays through the indemnity clause of the lease, or directly if its own shoveling made the ice worse.

claims.name: Customer falls on your wet floor or doorstep
claims.law: New York common law of premises liability (negligence); NYC Administrative Code §7-210 for the sidewalk; 29 CFR 1910.22(a) for workers
claims.trigger: entrance_floor_safety = nothing through a month with 8 or more wet days; at most one claim per year
claims.note: Not a government penalty: the record models a lawsuit so the engine can price the risk. Max $45,000 is the average slip, fall or customer injury claim of a small business in The Hartford's 2025 review (Insurance Journal, December 10, 2025); it was $20,000 in 2015. Base $2,500 is my planning value for what an insured owner pays: a $1,000-$2,500 deductible plus a premium increase at renewal. The claim arrives months after the fall: the New York deadline to sue for personal injury is three years (CPLR §214).

officials.name: Sanitation enforcement agent
officials.realProcess: Uniformed enforcement agents and sanitation police walk commercial blocks during set 'routing times' and after every snowfall. They write a summons on the spot to the business or the owner; no warning is required. The summons is answered at the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) or paid.

levers.name: Snow and ice at your door

options.label: Staff shovel and salt on the clock, within the legal window
Seasonal contract: a crew clears and salts after every snowfall
Leave it: the sun will melt it

levers.note: Charged only in December-March (activeMonths is a new field). Staff option: Central Park averages about 11 days a season with measurable snow (1991-2020 normals in ai/src/data/nyc-climate.json: Dec 2.1, Jan 3.7, Feb 3.2, Mar 2.0), about 2.75 a month; one hour of a $17.00 worker each time plus a second pass for refreeze = 2.75 x 1.5 h x $17 = $70, plus about $20 of ice melt. Contractor: no New York storefront price was found; vendor guides quote $350-$1,500 per visit for commercial lots in Brooklyn and $2,000-$10,000 a season nationally, which is plowing, not a 20-foot sidewalk. $400 a month ($1,600 a season) is my planning value for a shovel-only sidewalk contract: get three local quotes. The -3% demand of 'none' applies only on days with snow or ice on the ground (see extra.mechanics.sidewalk_clock).

levers.name: Wet floor at the entrance

options.label: Rented entrance mats swapped weekly, wet-floor signs, mop every hour in bad weather
A towel by the door

levers.note: No price list for mat rental in New York was found; $80 a month (two mats, weekly swap) is my planning value from uniform-service quotes I could not open. The reason the lever exists is the insurer's number: The Hartford's 2025 ten-year review puts the average slip, fall or customer injury claim of a small business at $45,000, up from $20,000 in 2015, and one in five small-business liability claims is now a fall.

levers.name: When a storm is forecast

options.label: Open as usual with the full schedule
Open with whoever lives close; cancel the other shifts the night before
Close on warning days and tell staff the evening before

levers.note: Applies only on days with a National Weather Service warning (blizzard, winter storm, flash flood, tropical storm). open_as_usual: full wages against 40% of normal traffic, and workers who cannot get in are simply absent. skeleton_crew: wages for half the staff; shifts cancelled the night before cost nothing. close_for_the_day: no sales and no wages if staff were told before they reported; anyone who already reported is owed call-in pay of 3 hours at the minimum wage (12 NYCRR §146-1.5; the State Labor Department applies it to weather closings). The effects written here are month-level placeholders: 1-2 warning days a month in winter. The shortcut storm_day_no_call_in_pay is the illegal variant.

levers.name: Trash: bins and pickups

options.label: Lidded bins, private carter three nights a week
Lidded bins, carter six nights a week
Black bags on the curb, no bins

levers.note: The pack already charges $250 a month for the carter (monthlyCosts.waste); the costs here are differences from it. Six pickups instead of three: no published New York price was found (each waste zone has its own maximum-rate table); +$180 is my planning value, about 70% more for twice the stops. Bags instead of bins saves only the bins: two 44-gallon rigid lidded bins at about $90 each replaced every year = $15 a month. Three pickups a week means food waste sits two nights: in June-September that feeds the rodent events (see extra.mechanics.trash_and_rodent_pressure).

levers.name: Your stretch of sidewalk

options.label: Sweep at opening and before closing, out to 18 inches into the street
Sweep twice a day and power-wash once a month
It is the city's sidewalk

levers.note: Sweeping: 10 minutes a day of a $17.00 worker x 30 days = $85. Power wash: $150 a visit is my planning value for a 20-foot storefront; no New York price list was found. The duty is real: DSNY makes owners and tenants clean the sidewalk and the gutter 18 inches into the street, even when someone else dropped the litter.

levers.name: Summer: air conditioning and the door

options.label: Air conditioner serviced in spring, door kept shut
Run it until it breaks

levers.note: Charged May-September. $60 a month = one spring service visit of about $300 spread over five months (planning value). 'unserviced' has no fine; it decides whether the heat_wave_ac_failure event hits this shop (rule 4: the breakdown follows from the choice, not from dice). Propping the door open with the air conditioning on is the shortcut ac_with_open_door.

levers.name: A sidewalk shed over your door

options.label: Wait for it to come down
Hang a temporary sign on the shed and light your entrance
Lawyer letter for a rent credit; report idle months to 311

levers.note: Only shown while a shed covers the storefront. Sign: the Buildings Department lets a business whose lawful sign is blocked put a temporary sign on the face of the shed directly in front of the storefront; $150 a month = a $1,200 banner and LED strip written off over 8 months (planning value). The +3% recovers about half of the measured loss (3.5-9.7% of weekly transactions). Rent credit: nothing in the law gives a tenant a credit for a shed; it is whatever the lease says. -5% of rent for a $250-a-month lawyer retainer is my estimate of a negotiated outcome, not a right. Local Law 48 of 2025 fines the building owner for months with no work, which is the tenant's leverage.

levers.name: When the street is torn up or the train is out

options.label: Change nothing
'We are open' signs at both corners, a punch card for regulars
Push pickup orders and delivery while the block is hard to reach

levers.note: Only shown during a street, subway or utility disruption. The city pays nothing for lost sales (Small Business Services FAQ, 2022), so the owner pays for any mitigation. $200 = printed signs and a 10th-drink-free card at about 1% of sales; +3% is my estimate of what it wins back out of a 10-22% loss. Delivery: $100 of listing promotion; delivery orders also pay the platform commission that the pack models elsewhere.

levers.name: Parade, fair or race on your street

options.label: A normal day
Extra barista, double pastry order, cups stocked the night before
Sell five fast items from the door, no seating

levers.note: Applies on announced event days only. $120 = one extra 7-hour shift at $17.00. Deliveries cannot reach a closed street, so stock arrives the day before. The capacity gains are month-level placeholders; on the day itself the window menu roughly doubles orders per hour (design value). The crowd is only worth what you can serve.

shortcuts.name: Do not clear the snow
shortcuts.what: Nobody shovels or salts your sidewalk after a snowfall. You save the labor. A sanitation agent can ticket you the same day, and if someone falls on your ice the claim follows you for three years.

shortcuts.name: Send staff home in a storm with no pay
shortcuts.what: You close an hour into the storm and pay only the minutes worked. The law says everyone who reported is owed at least three hours.

shortcuts.name: Trash bags on the curb, no bins
shortcuts.what: You skip the lidded bins and put black bags straight on the sidewalk. Since March 2024 every business must use bins with secure lids. Bags also feed the rats on your own block.

shortcuts.name: Use the corner litter basket instead of a carter
shortcuts.what: Staff carry the shop's trash to the city basket on the corner. You save the private carter's bill. City baskets are for pedestrians only, and a cup with your logo in the bag is all the proof an agent needs.

shortcuts.name: Everything in one bag
shortcuts.what: No sorting: cardboard, milk jugs and trash go out together and the carter charges less. Businesses must separate recyclables.

shortcuts.name: Tape flyers to lampposts
shortcuts.what: Fifty flyers on poles and construction fences instead of paid ads. Posting on public property is illegal, and each flyer is its own ticket.

shortcuts.name: A-frame sign and bench out in the walkway
shortcuts.what: You put the sandwich board and a bench where people have to walk around them. More passers-by notice the shop. Anything more than 3 feet from your wall is an obstruction.

shortcuts.name: Door propped open with the air conditioning on
shortcuts.what: An open door and a wave of cold air pull people in off a hot sidewalk. It is illegal for every store in the city, and it adds to your electric bill.

violations.name: Snow or ice left on the sidewalk past the legal deadline
violations.criminal: None. The larger exposure is civil: a pedestrian who falls on the uncleared sidewalk can sue the building owner (Administrative Code §7-210), and most store leases make the tenant pay the owner back.
violations.note: DSNY snow laws page as quoted by web search: snow that stops between 7:00 AM and 4:59 PM must be cleared within 4 hours; between 5:00 PM and 8:59 PM within 14 hours; between 9:00 PM and 6:59 AM by 11:00 AM. A path at least 4 feet wide where possible; snow may not be pushed into the street or crosswalk. Fines on that page: $100 first offense, $150 second, $250 third and later; a DSNY flyer and news reports give $100-$150, $150-$350 and $250-$350. The 2014 DSNY rules digest names 'every owner, lessee, tenant, occupant, or other person having charge of any lot or building'. Each uncleared snowfall is a new offense. After the January 25, 2026 storm (11.4 inches in Central Park) the city wrote more than 4,000 such summonses.

violations.name: Call-in pay not paid after a weather closing
violations.law: 12 NYCRR §146-1.5 (Hospitality Industry Wage Order); NY Labor Law §198(1-a)
violations.criminal: None for a first case; repeated willful non-payment of wages is a misdemeanor under Labor Law §198-a.
violations.note: Attorney General wage page as quoted by web search: in most cases restaurant or hotel workers should receive three hours of pay at the applicable minimum wage when they report and are sent home. Law firms report the State Labor Department applies call-in pay to closings for bad weather. Saved amount: one sent-home shift per worker per winter month, 3 h x $17.00 = $51, less about an hour actually paid = $35. Unpaid wages are owed back with 100% liquidated damages (Labor Law §198(1-a)), hence pctOfSaved 2, as for the other wage violations in the pack.

violations.name: Dirty sidewalk or gutter in front of the shop
violations.note: DSNY cleaning rules for businesses, as quoted by web search: owners and tenants must clean the sidewalk along the building and the gutter 18 inches from the curb into the street, including tree pits; $50 for the first offense. The Sanitation Foundation gives $100 for each later one; the penalty schedule caps the violation at $300. 311 adds that the rule applies even if someone else caused the mess. Agents ticket commercial blocks during fixed routing hours.

violations.name: Trash set out in bags or at the wrong time
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-120; DSNY commercial containerization and set-out rules (Title 16, Rules of the City of New York)
violations.note: DSNY, March 2024, as quoted by web search: starting March 1, 2024 all businesses must put trash in bins with secure lids; fines start at $50 for a first offense, $100 for a second and $200 for every one after. The business set-out page: bins go out one hour before closing or after 8:00 PM, come off the curb by the time the business reopens, and may be stored within 3 feet of the building line. Recycling in bags or bundles may go out after 8 PM. The exact rule section number was not confirmed.

violations.name: Business trash in a public litter basket
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-120(e); §16-116 (businesses must use a licensed private carter)
violations.note: DSNY collection and set-out laws for businesses, as quoted by web search: 'Under no circumstances can a merchant dispose of any garbage or recyclable materials in a DSNY litter basket'; $100 first offense, $250 second, $350 third and later. The code presumes that the person whose name appears on garbage found in the basket put it there.

violations.name: Recyclables not separated
violations.note: DSNY business pages as quoted by web search: $100 first offense, $200 second, $400 third and later for failing to separate recyclables. The section numbers are from memory and need a check against the code.

violations.name: Flyers posted on public property
violations.note: Each flyer is a separate violation: $75-$150 for a first offense and $150-$250 for later ones within 12 months (§10-121 as summarized in City Council Introduction 302 of 2024). Base $750 = ten flyers at $75. Max $9,000: a new pet shop in Clinton Hill was fined almost $9,000 for flyers announcing its opening (DNAinfo). The law presumes the business named on the flyer posted it.

violations.name: Sign, bench or goods blocking the sidewalk
violations.law: NYC Administrative Code §16-118 and §19-136 (sidewalk obstructions); 311 guidance: within 3 feet of the building
violations.note: 311, as quoted by web search: sandwich and A-frame signs must not extend more than 3 feet into the sidewalk from the building. Fine amounts are from press reports, not a current schedule: $100 for a first sign violation and up to $300 after (DSNY to the Midtown Gazette, 2015); a Brooklyn coffee shop was fined $300 by the Sanitation Department for a sidewalk sign (Fox News). The section numbers need a check.

violations.name: Air conditioning running with the door open
violations.note: DCWP business flyer as quoted by web search: 'The law prohibiting stores from leaving doors or windows open while air conditioning is running now applies to all stores regardless of size'; the only exception on the inspection checklist is a door open for deliveries. Press reports of the law give $250 for a first offense and up to $1,000. Enforcement is light: in 2023 DCWP made nearly 2,300 inspections and wrote 58 violations for open doors.

ruleCards.title: The snow clock
ruleCards.text: When snow stops between 7 AM and 4:59 PM you have 4 hours to clear your sidewalk; 5 PM to 8:59 PM, 14 hours; overnight, until 11 AM. A 4-foot path, nothing pushed into the street. Fines run $100 to $350 per snowfall.

ruleCards.title: Who pays when someone falls
ruleCards.text: In New York City the building owner, not the city, is liable when someone is hurt on the sidewalk in front (Administrative Code §7-210). Read your lease: most make the store clear the snow and pay the owner back. The average fall claim is $45,000.

ruleCards.title: Sending staff home in a storm
ruleCards.text: Close early for weather and you still owe pay: under New York's hospitality wage order a worker who reports for a shift is owed at least 3 hours at the minimum wage, or the scheduled shift if shorter. Decide before they travel, not after.

ruleCards.title: Bins with lids
ruleCards.text: Since March 1, 2024 every NYC business must set out trash in bins with secure lids: out one hour before closing or after 8 PM, back in before you reopen. Bags on the curb cost $50, then $100, then $200 each time.

ruleCards.title: 18 inches into the street
ruleCards.text: You must keep your sidewalk clean and the gutter too, 18 inches out from the curb, even if someone else dropped the litter. $50 the first time, $100 after that. Agents come during fixed hours for your block.

ruleCards.title: The corner basket is not yours
ruleCards.text: City litter baskets are for pedestrians. Shop trash in a basket costs $100, then $250, then $350, and a cup with your name on it is treated as proof. Every business must hire a licensed private carter.

ruleCards.title: Shut the door
ruleCards.text: No store in New York City may run air conditioning with its doors or windows open (Local Law 92 of 2015). The only exception is a door open for deliveries. Fines start at $250 and reach $1,000.

ruleCards.title: Sidewalk sheds
ruleCards.text: A shed over your door cuts restaurant and bar transactions by 3.5-9.7% a week. Since 2025 shed permits last 90 days, not a year, and owners pay monthly penalties when no work is done. You may hang a temporary sign on the shed in front of your store.

ruleCards.title: Nobody pays for the dig
ruleCards.text: When the city tears up your street, your sales are your problem. The City's own FAQ: it 'does not have any programs or grants to reimburse a business for lost revenue because of construction.' Ask about the project before you sign a lease.

ruleCards.title: A-frame signs
ruleCards.text: A sandwich board is tolerated only close to your wall: no more than 3 feet out from the building. Further out it is a sidewalk obstruction. Fines run $100 to $300, and a shed or a narrow sidewalk leaves you no legal spot at all.

ruleCards.title: Flyers on poles
ruleCards.text: Taping flyers to lampposts, mailboxes or fences is illegal posting: $75 to $150 for each flyer the first time, $150 to $250 after. Ten flyers is ten tickets. One new Brooklyn shop was fined almost $9,000.

ruleCards.title: Congestion Relief Zone
ruleCards.text: Below 60th Street in Manhattan cars pay $9 a day at peak hours; delivery trucks pay $14.40 or $21.60 every time they enter. Suppliers pass it on. In year one foot traffic in the zone rose 3.4% against 1.4% for the borough.

reports.name: Report a dirty sidewalk, trash bags or uncleared snow (311)
reports.text: The Sanitation Department sends an enforcement agent to the address. If the sidewalk is clean and the bins are out properly, you get a warning for a false report.

reports.name: Report a store cooling the street (311)
reports.text: Consumer and Worker Protection checks whether the door is propped open with the air conditioning on.

events.name: Sidewalk shed goes up on your block
events.text: Scaffolding covers your storefront while the building repairs its facade. Fewer people notice the shop, and nobody can tell you when it comes down.
events.note: Fix of the existing event (was 0.9 for 3 months, both my predecessor's estimates). The city's 2024 study with Mastercard: restaurants and bars under a shed saw weekly transactions fall 3.5-9.7% in the six months after it went up; Manhattan businesses lost $3,900-$9,500 a month. 0.93 is the midpoint (6.6%). Length: the average shed permit in March 2026 was 557 days old (West Side Rag analysis of Buildings Department data), so 12 months is still short; the engine caps an event at a season.
